sentences.text: The genus Invictibellatrix includes only one species, I. amberina, known from a single braincase fossil.
Scientists estimate this animal weighed between 200 and 300 kilograms and measured about 4 meters long.
A distinctive feature is the crest on the back of the skull, which has an hourglass shape and is lightly compressed from side to side.
The fossil material was found in the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight, United Kingdom.

Cassius Morrison and colleagues formally named the new genus and species in 2026, designating specimen NHMUK PV R 6775 as the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — after it was sold to the Natural History Museum in London in May 1924 by the widow of collector Reginald Walter Hooley.
Morrison et al. established the genus Invictibellatrix in 2026, placing it within the parent group Megaraptora.
Invictibellatrix lived during the Barremian stage, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago, in the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, UK, during the Barremian age of the Lower Cretaceous.
The discovery of Invictibellatrix adds to the known diversity of Early Cretaceous European coelurosaurs, which now includes tyrannosauroids, maniraptoriforms, and megaraptorans.
